food.text: During the early 19th century, American cooking was based mostly on what the farming population could grow, hunt, or raise on its own land. With more immigrants arriving and more people moving to city life, American food diversified further in the latter part of the century.

In the 1840 presidential election, disdain for fancy French cooking became a campaign issue. The Whig candidate William Henry Harrison was touted as living on "raw beef and salt", while a smear campaign targeted Martin Van Buren, who was known to have a taste for French cuisine.

Labor-saving machines changed how food was produced in the United States. The McCormick reaper (1834), the Pitts mechanical thresher (1837), and the Marsh harvester (1858) helped the country flood European cereal markets.

When the New York Hotel opened in 1844, it served meals a la carte, and local newspapers objected. They argued that offering different food at different prices attacked the foundations of the Republic. Nat P. Willis of the Weekly Mirror called the public table "the tangible republic".
The Campbell's Soup Company has been headquartered in Camden, New Jersey, since 1869. Its founding marked the start of the state's reputation for commercial food and industrial production.

Modern bannock recipes were shaped by government rations handed out on Indian reserves in the late 19th century, after the arrival of non-Indigenous settlers restricted Indigenous people's access to country foods (plants and animals native to the region). The rations were wheat flour, sugar, lard, and butter: high-calorie, low-nutrient, shelf-stable foods produced in bulk and shipped long distances. Under the reservation system Indigenous people were forced to give up much of their traditional food sources, and bannock became a necessary staple to feed their families and stave off starvation. These ingredients helped people survive that loss, but for some they remain a reminder of the negative impacts of colonialism and are regarded as an imposition.

Travelers of the era often complained about the food they found. Thomas Hamilton recorded in 1803 that between New Orleans and Charleston they were beyond the region of bread, eating eggs, broiled venison, and fried cakes of Indian corn. James Creecy lived on salt pork and "musty corn meal dodgers" for weeks.

Pork roll is a sausage-like pork product developed by John Taylor in Trenton in the late 19th century. In North Jersey it is usually called Taylor Ham. It is generally eaten sliced and grilled, often in a sandwich with a fried egg and American cheese.

Scandinavian immigrants brought 19th-century dishes such as lutefisk and egg coffee to Minnesota. These have either substantially decreased in popularity or entirely disappeared in Scandinavia itself, while they remain common in Minnesota.

Camas bulbs, out of which bannocks can be made, contributed to the survival of members of the Lewis and Clark Expedition (1804-06). Native American tribes who ate camas include the Nez Perce, Cree, Coast Salish, and Blackfoot.

Antebellum cooking left a few casualties. Seminole soup, made with squirrel, and turtle soup have vanished from modern American cuisine. Macaroni a la cardinale became popular in the late 19th century but was completely unknown in the Antebellum era.

art.text: From 1820, the Hudson River School began producing Romantic landscape paintings that were original and matched the huge scale of U.S. landscapes. It was one of the first signs that American artists were finding a voice of their own.
art.source_title: Visual art of the United States

art.text: The American craft movement took shape in rural parts of the United States as a reaction to the Industrial Revolution. Makers turned to handwork at the moment machines were taking over production.
art.source_title: Visual art of the United States

art.text: After 1850, Academic art in the European style flourished in the United States. As richer Americans became very wealthy, European art, both new and old, began flowing to the country, and museums opened to display much of it.
art.source_title: Visual art of the United States

art.text: Western American art often depicted cowboys, Native Americans, horses and scenic landscapes. Its artists tended to focus more on subject and narrative than on style. After the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, artists and explorers were inspired to enter the West.
The 1913 Armory Show in New York City brought developments in European modern art to the United States. Such exhibitions were how new European ideas reached American audiences.
art.source_title: Visual art of the United States

art.text: George Catlin gave up a law career and began drawing portraits of Indians from more than 50 tribes. He also recorded hunting scenes, tribal rituals and landscapes, and his paintings later became valued as historical resources because of the accuracy of their details.

George Caleb Bingham (1811 to 1879) painted elections in the 1850s that historians now use to explain the details of grassroots democracy. The paintings toured for years, as Americans paid money to see themselves in political action.
art.source_title: American election campaigns in the 19th century

art.text: In the United States, "Victorian" architecture generally describes styles most popular between 1860 and 1900. These include Second Empire, Stick-Eastlake, Folk Victorian, Queen Anne, Richardsonian Romanesque and Shingle.

From the 1830s to 1850s, paintings tended to present Native Americans as "noble savages". As conflicts between white settlers and Indians grew around mid-century, the portrayal became more negative, shifting from "noble red men" to hostile savages.

Jacob Wrey Mould, Chief Architect of Public Works in New York City, was among the prominent architects who produced English-derived designs around the world. Magazines such as The Builder helped colonial architects keep informed about current fashion.

The Arnold Print Works in North Adams, Massachusetts, was one of the world's leading producers of printed textiles. At its 1905 peak it employed more than 3,000 workers and produced 580,000 yards of cloth per week. Its factory buildings, built between 1870 and 1900, later became the MASS MoCA museum.

Stick-Eastlake was a manner of geometric, machine-cut decorating derived from Stick and Queen Anne. It is sometimes considered a distinct style. Terms like "Painted Ladies" or "gingerbread" describe certain Victorian buildings but are not specific styles.

war.text: The United States declared war on Britain on 18 June 1812, objecting to British trade restrictions and the Royal Navy's impressment of seamen from American vessels. Votes for war in the House and Senate divided along strict party lines, with the Democratic-Republican Party in favour and the Federalist Party against.

The Mexican-American War (1846-1848) was an invasion of Mexico by the United States. It followed the 1845 American annexation of Texas, which Mexico still considered its territory. Mexico suffered large losses of life in both its military and civilian population, and by the end it had lost more than half of its territory.

Gall, a Hunkpapa Lakota war chief, was an important military leader at the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876. A reassessment based on battlefield excavations and Native oral histories has given him greater credit for crucial tactical decisions in the Sioux and Cheyenne's overpowering defeat of the five companies of Custer's 7th Cavalry. The warriors finished off Custer and his men, and the last approximately 28 survivors, who made a dash south for the river, were trapped in the box canyon called "Deep Ravine" and killed. The Indians had completely annihilated Custer's five companies.

The Royal Navy's blockade of the United States began informally in the late fall of 1812 under Admiral John Borlase Warren. Twenty ships were on station in 1812, and 135 were in place by the end of the conflict.

The boundary between Texas and Mexico was disputed before the Mexican-American War. The Republic of Texas and the U.S. asserted it was the Rio Grande, while Mexico claimed the more northerly Nueces River.

After war was declared on May 13, 1846, General Stephen W. Kearny moved southwest from Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, in June 1846 with about 1,700 men in his Army of the West. His orders were to secure the territories of Nuevo México and Alta California.

The Whitman massacre of 1847 triggered the Cayuse War, which led to fighting from the Cascade Range to the Rocky Mountains. The conflict expanded into the Yakama War (1855-1858), and then the Puget Sound War of 1855-1856, remembered for the Battle of Seattle and the execution of Nisqually Chief Leschi.

The Royal Navy tightened its blockade until it covered the entire American coast on 31 May 1814. In May 1814, after Napoleon's abdication and the end of supply problems with Wellington's army, New England was blockaded as well.

The War of 1812 cost the United States $90 million, peaking at 2.7% of GDP. The national debt rose from $45 million in 1812 to $127 million by the end of 1815, yet by selling bonds and notes at deep discounts the government received only $34 million worth of specie.

In February 1847, Mexican conservatives rebelled against the liberal government's attempt to take Church property to fund the war effort. In the Revolt of the Polkos, the Catholic Church and conservatives paid soldiers to rise up, forcing Santa Anna to leave his campaign and return to the capital.
Major Marcus Reno's initial attack on the southeast end of the Native American village killed Gall's two wives and several children. Gall later said, "My heart was very bad that day."

Stephen Girard, the richest man in the United States at the time, was among those who funded the American government's involvement in the War of 1812. The war added some £25 million to Britain's national debt.

literature.text: In the early-to-mid-19th century, the writer and critic John Neal helped push America toward a unique literature and culture. He criticized predecessors such as Washington Irving for imitating their British counterparts, and he influenced writers such as Edgar Allan Poe.

Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter appeared in 1850. It is a drama set in Puritan Massachusetts about a woman cast out of her community for committing adultery with a minister who refuses to acknowledge his own sin. Herman Melville's Moby-Dick followed in 1851, and both books explored the dark aspects of human nature.

David Walker's Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World came out in 1829, and Frederick Douglass published his Narrative in 1845. Harriet Jacobs followed with Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl in 1861. Jacobs' account disclosed specific injustices that Black women suffered under slavery, especially sexual harassment and the threat or actual perpetration of rape as a tool of slavery.

Edgar Allan Poe was born in Boston but raised in Virginia. In 1832 he began writing short stories such as "The Fall of the House of Usher" that explore hidden depths of human psychology. His "The Murders in the Rue Morgue" is seen as the first detective story.
tags: The Fall of the House of Usher
The Murders in the Rue Morgue

literature.text: Victor Séjour, born free in New Orleans, moved to France at 19 and published the short story "Le Mulâtre" in 1837. It is the first known work of fiction by an African American. Because it was written in French and printed in a French journal, it apparently had no influence on later American literature.

Paul Laurence Dunbar, who often wrote in the rural, black dialect of the day, was the first African American poet to gain national prominence. His first book of poetry, Oak and Ivy, was published in 1893.

The earliest known Native-authored play is Wep-Ton-No-Mah, written in 1892 by the Seneca actress and playwright Gowongo Mohawk. It was performed in the United Kingdom, marking a rare case of 19th-century Indigenous authorship and international performance.
Omar ibn Said, a Muslim slave in the Carolinas, wrote an autobiography in Arabic in 1831. It is considered an early example of African-American literature.

John Neal's 1828 novel Rachel Dyer was the earliest use of the Salem witch trials as the basis for a novel. He had already published several books in the 1820s, including Logan in 1822 and Seventy-Six in 1823.

George Tucker produced the first fiction of Virginia colonial life in 1824 with The Valley of Shenandoah. In 1827 he followed it with A Voyage to the Moon, one of the country's first science fictions, about the people of Morosofia.

Mohawk poet Emily Pauline Johnson gave dramatic readings in the 1890s that blurred the boundaries between poetry, storytelling, and theatrical presence. Her late 19th-century tours helped popularize Indigenous narratives.

Paul Laurence Dunbar's When Malindy Sings, published in 1906, includes photographs taken by the Hampton Institute Camera Club. Along with Joggin' Erlong, also from 1906, it gives revealing glimpses into the lives of rural African Americans of the day.

The Kensington Runestone, found in Minnesota in 1898, carries an inscription purporting to record Scandinavian explorers in the 14th century, internally dated to 1362. The text says eight Geats and twenty-two Norwegians returned from a day of fishing to find ten of their men "red of blood and dead", and it includes a prayer to be saved from evil. Since the first scientific examination in 1910, scholarly consensus has classified it as a 19th-century hoax, with some critics charging Olof Ohman, who reported finding it, with fabrication.

science.text: The Industrial Revolution reached the United States in two phases. The first ran from the late 18th century through the first half of the 19th century, and the second advanced after the American Civil War. Together they moved the U.S. economy from manual labor, farm labor and handicraft work toward industrialization based on wage labour.
science.source_title: Industrial Revolution in the United States

science.text: The First Industrial Revolution began in the late 18th century, but it expanded beyond its British homeland for the first time during the 19th century. Among the places it remade was the Northeastern United States, alongside the Low Countries, France, the Rhineland and Northern Italy.

Samuel Slater introduced British industrial methods in textile manufacturing to the United States, and Eli Whitney's 1794 invention of the cotton gin gave American slaveholders the means to make cotton production significantly more profitable. By the mid-19th century, southern slave plantations supplied 75% of the world's cotton, and the planter class saw clear gains in productivity among their slaves. Both men are named among the main contributors to the First Industrial Revolution in America.
science.source_title: Industrial Revolution in the United States

science.text: Éleuthère Irénée du Pont, whose family emigrated during the French Revolution bringing expertise in chemistry and gunpowder, observed that American gunpowder was of poor quality. In 1802 he opened the Eleutherian Mills powder mill in Wilmington, Delaware.
science.source_title: Industrial Revolution in the United States

science.text: The Eleutherian Mills served as home for the du Pont family and as a center of business and social life, with employees living at or near the mill. The company grew rapidly, and by the mid-19th century it had become the largest supplier of gunpowder to the United States military.
science.source_title: Industrial Revolution in the United States

science.text: The Erie Canal, built between 1817 and 1821, is listed among the main contributors to the First Industrial Revolution in the United States. So are other industrial advancements that were necessitated by the War of 1812.
science.source_title: Industrial Revolution in the United States

science.text: The U.S. share of global manufacturing rose from 23% in 1870 to 36% in 1913. Economic historian Douglas Irwin notes that high tariffs cost around 0.5% of GDP in the mid-1870s, and that growth was driven more by abundant resources and openness to people and ideas.
science.source_title: Industrial Revolution in the United States

politics.text: Historians identify three waves of migration to the United States. About five million people came between 1815 and 1860, some 10 million between 1865 and 1890, and 15 million between 1890 and 1914. The last wave came mainly from central, eastern, and southern Europe.

The 1803 Louisiana Purchase transferred 828,000 square miles of territory claimed by France to the United States. Via the 1846 to 1848 Mexican-American War, the United States annexed another 525,000 square miles of Mexican territory. In 1867, the Andrew Johnson administration bought Alaska from Russia.

After the War of 1812, the Treaty of 1818 set the 49th parallel as the border between the United States and British North America, running west to the Rocky Mountains. In 1846 a second treaty split the jointly administered Oregon Country and extended that line west to the Puget Sound.

The Indian Removal Act of 1830 forced tribes such as the Cherokee and the Choctaw to move out of their homelands, so that the land could be sold to European Americans. Native Americans who resisted relocation were drawn into conflicts such as the Second Seminole War, which caused the deaths of 3,000 Native Americans. Those who were moved were confined to isolated reservations, often unsuitable for the subsistence farming they were pushed to take up, and became dependent on the U.S. government for annuities and supplies.

In 1823 President James Monroe promulgated the Monroe Doctrine in order to end European interventions in Latin America. Territorial expansion was explicit in the 19th century idea of manifest destiny.

In 1893, with support from marines from the USS Boston, Queen Lili'uokalani of Hawaii was deposed in a bloodless coup. She had succeeded her brother King Kalākaua in 1891. Hawaii became a US territory and later the 50th state in 1959.

In 1870, Rupert's Land, the territory of the Hudson's Bay Company, was annexed to Canada as the North-West Territories and the new province of Manitoba. British Columbia joined as the sixth province in 1871, and Prince Edward Island became the seventh in 1873.

The Trail of Tears was the ethnic cleansing and forced displacement of approximately 60,000 people of the Five Civilized Tribes between 1830 and 1850. The relocated peoples suffered from exposure, disease and starvation on the way, and thousands, made vulnerable by removal, died of disease before reaching their destinations or shortly after. Historians such as David Stannard and Barbara Mann have noted that the army deliberately routed the Cherokee march through areas of a known cholera epidemic, such as Vicksburg, Mississippi. Stannard estimates that 8,000 Cherokee died during the forced removal, about half the total population.
politics.source_title: Native American genocide in the United States

politics.text: Lincoln issued a preliminary Emancipation Proclamation on September 22, 1862, warning that slaves in states still in rebellion on January 1, 1863, would be declared free. The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in 1865, officially abolished slavery in the entire country.

The 1848 Revolutions brought more German immigration to America with the Forty-eighters, several of whom read philosophy and supported the Union Army. Among them was Carl Schurz, while Fritz Anneke and Joseph Weydemeyer were Marxist revolutionaries who served as Union officers.

On July 6, 1887, the Hawaiian League, an illegal secret society, threatened King David Kalākaua, Hawaii's last king. It forced him to enact a new constitution that stripped him of much of his power. He had signed a treaty with the US in 1885 allowing tariff-free sugar exports to the US mainland.

The American Colonization Society, a private organization, began subsidizing free black Americans to colonize the west coast of Africa in 1820. In 1822 it established the colony of Liberia, which became independent in 1847.

The 1863 Emancipation Proclamation applied only to states in rebellion and did not legally affect slavery in Native American areas that fought for the Confederacy. All slaves were legally emancipated upon ratification of the 13th Amendment on December 6, 1865. In 1866 the federal government negotiated new treaties with the Five Civilized Tribes, in which they agreed to end slavery.

The boundary of British Columbia with Washington Territory was settled by arbitration in 1872. Its boundary with Alaska was settled by arbitration in 1903. Britain also ceded the Arctic Archipelago to Canada in 1880.

philosophy.text: A small number of 19th century philosophies are known as uniquely American in origin: pragmatism and transcendentalism. Their most prominent proponents were William James and Ralph Waldo Emerson respectively.

Harvard's philosophy teaching shifted from conservative religious traditions to more liberal schools of thought. Early in the 19th century it was associated with the development of unitarianism and, correspondingly, transcendentalism. It produced thinkers like Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau.

Alexander Stephens gave the Cornerstone Speech, stating that slavery was the cornerstone of the Confederacy. Slavery also found intellectual defenders in the South, and the philosophical defense of it became a significant part of Confederate thought.

In 1805, Harvard appointed the first unitarian professor of divinity. Afterward the school became dominated by a unitarian moral philosophy that rejected Christ's divinity and departed from the orthodox theology of earlier Puritans. Transcendentalism followed, emphasizing free conscience and the value of intellectual reason.

Josiah Royce, a Harvard philosopher, was the most prominent advocate of American idealism. He wrote that "the world is...such stuff as ideas are made of." His works include The Religious Aspect of Philosophy (1885) and The Problem of Christianity (1913).

The Ghost Dance movement originated among the Paiute in 1889 and spread throughout the Great Plains. By 1890 it had attracted growing popularity among the Lakota. U.S. authorities tried to suppress it, killed Sitting Bull while trying to arrest its leaders, and tensions led to the Massacre at Wounded Knee in 1890.

In the early decades of the 19th century, Harvard's philosophy curriculum was dominated by Scottish common sense realism and the empiricism of John Locke. Required readings included works by Thomas Brown, William Paley and Dugald Stewart. The college also required professors to declare allegiance to the Protestant Reformed Christian faith.

Josiah Royce was a student of Peirce at Johns Hopkins, and he published in the Journal of Speculative Philosophy. His The World and the Individual appeared in volumes from 1899 to 1901, and The Philosophy of Loyalty in 1908.

George Fitzhugh, a leading pro-slavery intellectual influenced by Thomas Carlyle, rebuked Franklin, Locke, Smith and the entire liberal tradition in Sociology for the South (1854) and Cannibals All! (1857). He preferred feudalism instead.

Albert Taylor Bledsoe wrote Liberty and Slavery in 1856, described as the most extensive philosophical treatment of slavery ever produced by a Southern academic. Lost Cause advocates still cite it. James Henley Thornwell likewise advocated slavery and a "metaphysical" Confederacy.

culture.text: The Second Great Awakening, especially in the period 1800–1840, converted millions to evangelical Protestantism. It came as cultivation of the highly profitable cotton crop exploded in the Deep South after 1820, and with it the use of slave labor. In the North it energized multiple social reform movements, including abolitionism, while in the South, Methodists and Baptists proselytized among slave populations.

The Native American Church, also known as Peyotism, is a syncretic religion that combines traditional Native American beliefs with elements of Christianity. It originated in the Oklahoma Territory in the late nineteenth century, after peyote was introduced to the southern Great Plains from Mexico.

Professional baseball dates from 1869, and baseball is the oldest of the major American team sports. It had no close rivals in popularity until the 1960s, and it is still referred to as "the national pastime".

Nineteenth-century fashion in Europe and North America reflected the era's technology, art and politics. Women's styles displayed the female silhouette with corset-pinched waistlines and bustling full skirts. Men wore three-piece suits tailored for usefulness in business as well as sporting activity.

Victor Griffin, known as the last chief of the Quapaw tribe, was noted for facilitating the incorporation of the Native American Church under Oklahoma law in 1911. He also helped spread the religion to some other related tribes in the region.

Native American Church ceremonies commonly last all night, beginning Saturday evening and ending early Sunday morning. They include scripture reading, prayer, singing, and drumming. The church believes in one supreme God, the Great Spirit, and in the Trinity.

As standards of living slowly improved and income per capita rose, the middle class began to spend more on indulgent rather than solely necessary goods. Telegraphy and new railways connected people in major industrial cities to one another.

The nobleman and scientist Maximilian zu Wied-Neuwied traveled to North America from 1832 to 1834, accompanied by the Swiss painter Karl Bodmer. Bodmer's portraits of Indians of North Dakota, the Ohio River and the Missouri River include Blackfoot, Choctaw, Cherokee and Chickasaw subjects.
culture.source_title: Native Americans in German popular culture

culture.text: The original 1913 charter of the Native American Church of the United States was enabled in Oklahoma territory. Chapters with this designation have no blood quantum requirements to attend ceremonies, and all races are generally welcome.
Buffalo Bill's European shows in 1890 and between 1903 and 1907 involved several hundred Indians. The shows were quite popular in Germany.
culture.source_title: Native Americans in German popular culture

culture.text: Edward Two-Two, a Lakota-Sioux, worked at the Sarrasani circus in Dresden in 1913/14. He was buried there in 1914 according to his wishes.
culture.source_title: Native Americans in German popular culture
